wacc.formula: WACC = wₑ × kₑ + w_d × k_d × (1 − t);  kₑ = r_f + β × ERP
steps: β (Blume-adjusted) = 0.67 × raw β — + 0.33 = 1.00  (fewer than 52 weeks of prices: beta 1.0 assumed)
k_d = 7.10%  (10-year Treasury + 2% (no rate on file)); after tax 7.10% × (1 − 21%) = 5.61%

methods.formula: Value per share = (peer median EV/Sales × Revenue − net debt) ÷ shares
methods.fit: It has revenue ($3.22B over four quarters) — the measure that still works without profit, and 29 peers (SIC 3841) have the multiple.

methods.formula: Value = book + Σ (ROEₜ − kₑ) × Bookₜ₋₁ ÷ (1 + kₑ)ᵗ over 10 years; ROE fades linearly to kₑ; half of earnings retained
methods.fit: Equity is positive ($3.62B) and so is net income (−$314.0M), so the return it earns on book value can be compared with what shareholders require.

methods.formula: Value per share = (1 − p) × going-concern value + p × liquidation value
steps: p(fail within 5 years) = clamp(0.5 − runway 0.9 years ÷ 10, 5%, 50%) = 40.8%
inputs: SEC XBRL frames: diluted weighted-average shares
assumptions: no distress estimate: from the cash runway (an assumption)
an assumption for a forced sale
methods.fit: It is burning cash (free cash flow −$225.0M a year, a runway of 0.9 years), so its value must allow for the chance it does not survive.

methods.formula: Stage-weighted value = Σ weight × central value of the stage's methods (weights renormalized over the methods available)
assumptions: fixed by stage before any result was seen (base_rates.STAGES)
methods.fit: Its stage is “Decline / turnaround” — operating income ≤ 0, revenue growth unknown — which fixes these methods and their weights in advance.

methods.formula: Net current asset value per share = (current assets − total liabilities − other claims) ÷ shares;  a net-net trades below two-thirds of it
inputs: SEC XBRL frames: diluted weighted-average shares
assumptions: Fixed assets, goodwill, the business itself
Graham, Security Analysis (1934): a liquidation floor
methods.fit: Its current assets and liabilities are on file. Net-nets are rare among large companies; a positive figure is a floor that ignores everything the business owns beyond working capital.
